extracted.intended_audience: military contracting officers, judge advocates, and military administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Authoritative guidance on government contracting (acceptance, bidder rights, international carriage clauses, liability for work) and on the law of desertion (definition, evidence, apprehension, rewards, restoration, removal of charge). Intended to guide decisions and drafting in military administration and legal practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of nonconforming installed component contingent on bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: A cylinder installed in a steamer constructed for the Government did not meet the tests required by the contract, but it was probable that the cylinder as installed would continue to prove satisfactory. It was held there was no legal objection to accepting the cylinder as installed upon the contractor filing with the department a bond guaranteed by a surety conditioned to replace the cylinder and pay for the hire of a substitute vessel in the event it was necessary to replace the cylinder within two years and upon the contractor further giving his sole bond to cover the remaining period of the natural life of the cylinder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of nonconforming work may be lawful when remedial guarantees are provided: require a surety bond to replace defective work within a fixed period and to compensate for substitute hire, plus contractor's bond to cover the remaining life. (C. 26577, Apr. 22, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidder's right to choose officers to execute contract papers
rubrics_metrics.description: When a contract is awarded, the bidder has a right to go before officers of his own choosing (if they are of a class of officers such as the Government requires) and execute his bond and make his affidavit, etc., and submit them to the Government officers for acceptance. The Government officer has not the right to call him before a particular official of his choosing to execute the necessary papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracting officers should accept properly executed documents from qualified officials selected by the contractor; they may not compel appearance before a specific government official when the contractor uses officers of the required class. (C. 167, Aug. 18, 1894.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract clause for transporting troops through foreign territory
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause should be inserted in the contract requiring the company to obtain the written consent of the Canadian Government to the transportation of United States troops through Canadian territory, and that in case such permission should be refused the troops should be carried to their destination by another route without additional expense to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For carriage of troops across foreign territory, include an express contractual obligation to secure host-nation consent and a fallback routing obligation protecting the Government from extra expense if consent is denied. (C. 14552, Dec. 18, 1903, Jan. 19, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract clauses for transporting supplies through foreign territory
rubrics_metrics.description: Although international law does not require consent for passage of supplies in the ordinary course of commerce, as a matter of precaution insert a clause that any duties or impositions in the nature of customs dues should be paid by the contractor and should not become a charge against the United States; where conditions are unsettled also require contractor to make good any loss to property resulting from political or other disturbances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When routing supplies through foreign territory, require the contractor to bear customs duties and to be contractually liable for losses from political disturbances—protecting Government from incidental charges and risks. (C. 14552; C. 28430, May 26, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor liability for damages from blasting operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where blasting carried on in execution of a Government contract for rock excavation near a military post injured plastering, and it appeared the blasting was carried on with reasonable care, held that in the absence of facts showing that the performance of the contract by blasting was not contemplated by the parties, or that the contractor assumed responsibility for damages to the United States as the result of its operations, no recovery could be had against the contractor for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracting officers should determine whether the method of performance (e.g., blasting) was contemplated by the contract or whether the contractor assumed responsibility; reasonable care in performance is a defense to liability absent express assumption or unforeseen risk allocation. (C. 27673, Jan. 23, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment despite pending patent infringement suit when Government owns property
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the United States owns a piece of property and is in peaceable possession of it, the Government cannot be enjoined by courts and prevented from using it for Government purposes; thus, after an electric plant had been constructed under contract and suit later brought against the contractor for patent infringement asking that the commanding officer be enjoined from using the plant, it was held there was no objection to making payment to the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the Government owns and occupies the property, payment to contractors may proceed even if a third party sues for patent infringement, because courts will not enjoin Government use in such circumstances. (Belknap v. Schild cited; C. 716, Apr. 17, 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright ownership of official works
rubrics_metrics.description: The author or proprietor of a literary work is the only one who can legally copyright it. Held that a retired Army officer who purchased electrotype plates was not authorized to copyright them; an official of the War Department could not copyright in his own name a compilation of facts derived from records the property of the United States; an officer may not copyright a book which he prepares under orders from competent authority and which, after submission to a board of officers and slight revision, is approved by the Secretary of War for publication to and use by the Army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government personnel generally cannot claim copyright in works made under official orders or compilations from government records; private purchasers of government plates do not acquire copyright simply by purchase. (Cases and statutes cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of desertion: two elements required
rubrics_metrics.description: The offense of desertion is committed by an officer or enlisted man who absents himself without authority from the military service with the intent not to return thereto. The offense becomes complete when the intent not to return has been fully formed, and the party has committed an overt act looking toward his separation from the military service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution/administration must prove both (1) unauthorized voluntary withdrawal and (2) intent permanently to abandon the service; intent may be inferred from circumstances and duration of absence. (C. 15257, May 9, 1910; C. 9787, Feb. 7, 1901.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard: intent may be inferred from circumstances and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Both elements of desertion must be proved. The intent may be inferred not from the fact of absenting alone, but from the circumstances attending the fact, and the duration of the absence. An unauthorized absence of a few hours may be sufficient evidence of such intent, while an absence for a considerable interval unattended by circumstances indicating purpose to separate permanently may be proof simply of absence without leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each case is fact-specific; adjudicators must assess surrounding circumstances (escape, duration, acts like enlisting elsewhere) to infer intent; no universal temporal cutoff exists. (Various decisions cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Desertion distinct from mere absence from post or station
rubrics_metrics.description: Desertion does not necessarily include the offense of absence from station. For example, leaving one's company/barracks and proceeding to another barracks at the same station where men are being enlisted for foreign service and enlisting there without a discharge may be a desertion even though technically not absence from post or station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators must distinguish absence without leave from desertion by focusing on intent and the nature of acts (e.g., enlisting elsewhere) rather than only technical absence-from-post elements. (C. 24722, Apr. 5, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Escape as evidence of desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that a soldier escapes from confinement is not proof of desertion, since he may have had a minor object; but an escape followed by a considerable absence, especially if the soldier is obliged to be forcibly apprehended, is strong presumptive evidence of intent necessary to constitute the crime. An escape with intent to quit the service is a subsequent or additional desertion. Escape from legal military custody where the party is no longer in the military service cannot constitute desertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat escape and subsequent conduct as indicators of intent; brief escapes for ephemeral purposes do not automatically establish desertion, but prolonged absence or evasive conduct after escape strengthens the inference. (Multiple decisions cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and limits on apprehension of deserters
rubrics_metrics.description: As much force may be used as is necessary to apprehend deserters. Any forcible entry into a private dwelling that would be warranted by state law would be sustained by federal courts. Once arrest is made, the police officer may take the prisoner beyond his jurisdiction. The arresting officer need not obey a writ of habeas corpus of a state court but should reply giving a reason for non-compliance. Civilians may, upon request of the military, arrest deserters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military and cooperating civilian authorities have broad powers to apprehend deserters consistent with state law standards for forcible entry; procedures should include prompt judicial replies when state process is involved and formal requests when civilian arrest is sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for payment of rewards for delivery of deserters
rubrics_metrics.description: A reward may be paid for delivery of a deserter in a variety of situations: when he is charged with desertion; when administratively shown to be a deserter in fact; if convicted of absence without leave only; upon administrative establishment even if later discharged on habeas corpus; to recruiting officers or civilians when authorized; to multiple persons jointly; and even for second deliveries in some cases. The amount of the reward is that authorized at the date of apprehension and is in full for all services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify authorization conditions before paying rewards; note payability to multiple deliverers jointly by check, to various classes of deliverers (civilians, Indian police, Canadian detectives), and that the payable amount is fixed at date of apprehension. (Detailed list items V.A–V.B.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations where reward is not payable
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewards are not to be paid for partial performance, for merely giving notice of location without delivery, without delivery, for apprehension of a man discharged without honor (except by mistake), when a deserter is arrested abroad without authority, when extradited on other charges, when delivered to civil custody without request, or where there is evidence of collusion or no evidence of desertion; no reimbursement for damages/expenses if wrong man arrested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimants for reward must have effected proper delivery under authorized circumstances; exclude cases of partial performance, mere information, wrong person, or improper custody/authority. (Detailed list items V.F and subitems.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoppage and forfeiture of rewards and expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoppage of reward may be made upon conviction (of desertion or where sentence so directs). Stoppage of reward, expense of apprehension, etc., and original payment of reward are distinct transactions. Expenses of apprehension and transportation may be charged against a convicted deserter (transportation and commutation of rations of self and guard), but expense of returning deserter from place of delivery to proper station is not included in reward and usually limited to the shortest route.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish reward payments from reimbursable apprehension/transport expenses; ensure rules for stoppage upon conviction and limits on chargeable costs are followed. (Section V.D and related subitems.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration to duty without trial and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no legal objection if a deserter surrenders and is restored to duty without trial; application should be by the company commander. Restoration to duty without trial does not operate as an acquittal to remove the charge; it is treated as a constructive pardon in some contexts but does not preclude later administrative or statutory consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use company-command applications for restoration; record that restoration without trial is not equivalent to acquittal for purposes of removing charge unless specific statutory/administrative action is taken. (Sections XII and related items.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of charge procedures and grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary may remove a charge of desertion (e.g., decide service honest/faithful for reenlistment purposes). A charge may be removed by an honorable discharge, because it was erroneously made (prisoner of war, insane soldier, postal failures, furlough mistakes), or under special acts of Congress subject to statutory conditions (e.g., act of March 2, 1899; act of May 17, 1886). Restoration to duty without trial does not remove the charge; finding of not guilty by an illegal court-martial does not remove the charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow statutory criteria and administrative procedure for removal; check whether service meets honesty/faithfulness standards and whether statutory/time restrictions or act-specific limitations apply before removing a charge. (Sections XVI, XVII and statutory references.)
